html:
The Sanctuary of Asclepius at Epidaurus, in the northeast Peloponnese, was the main holy site of Asclepius, the Greek god of healing. Its great temple was built in the early 4th century BCE, and it drew sick people from all over the Greek world.

Patients bathed, made offerings and then slept in a long hall called the abaton. They hoped the god would come to them in a dream and heal them or tell them what to do; priests then helped carry out the advice. Stone tablets set up at the site record cures, some ordinary and some miraculous.

The sanctuary was rich and grand. Beside the temple stood a round building, the tholos, and guest houses, baths and a stadium. Its most famous building is the Theatre of Epidaurus.

The cult spread from here. Athens brought Asclepius to the city in 420 BCE, and Rome brought him to an island in the Tiber in 293 BCE after a plague. Greek temple healing grew up next to the more practical medicine of Hippocrates and the Hippocratic Oath, which begins by swearing by Asclepius. The site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988.
